tasks.text:
Every project review in our department begins with the same question: what actually went wrong? Last spring the team spent four weeks arguing about the budget, and it was that argument that delayed the launch. The budget itself was never the real problem. What the reviewers finally identified was a single missing test, a fault so small that nobody had considered it salient. It is this pattern, rather than any shortage of money, that explains most of our failures.
Since then we have changed the way we open a review. What we look for first is the crux of the problem, not the loudest complaint in the room. It was our new director who insisted on the rule, and her reasoning was simple. If a team cannot name the underlying cause in one sentence, it does not yet understand it. Trivial details are still recorded, but they are set aside; what receives attention is the decisive factor. The change has been substantial. Reviews that once consumed a whole afternoon now take under an hour, and the conclusions we reach are far more definitive.

tasks.text:
For almost a century the manuscript in the city museum was believed to have been written in 1420. That date is printed in every guidebook, and until recently nobody had tried to substantiate it. Last year a team from the university was reported to have found a second copy in a private collection. The second copy is thought to have been produced by the same workshop, yet its paper is clearly younger.
The old claim was quickly denounced by two historians, who pointed out that the earlier date had never been documented anywhere. Their objection is now widely cited. The museum, however, is said to have refused every new test, and its director is understood to have called the whole question unimportant.
Since then a small laboratory has been allowed to examine a single page. The results are believed to have corroborated the historians. The manuscript is now supposed to have been copied around 1560, more than a hundred years later than the label in the hall still claims. The museum has not corrected that label.

Having worked on the same river project for three years, the planning group finally presented its report last month. Being aware of the public interest, the city published the whole document online the same evening.
The report comprises four parts. Having studied the older plans first, the authors decided to begin with history. Their account, drawing on maps from the last century, shows how the two districts on either bank slowly diverged. Being separated by the water and by a busy road, the two neighbourhoods developed almost independently.
The second part encompasses transport. Having counted the traffic for six months, the team argues that a new bridge would entail far higher costs than a ferry. The third part, being the shortest of all, deals with parks.
Having read every comment received in April, the council will vote in June. Officials say that, being a long-term plan, the project must survive several changes of government. Whatever is decided, the debate is expected to culminate in a public meeting at the end of the year.

tasks.text:
Our editor has one rule, and every new writer soon learns it: if a word can be omitted, omit it. She never explains the rule twice, and she does not need to. Her marks in the margin are short, and so are her comments.
Last week she returned my article with three lines crossed out. You have said this already, she wrote, so do not restate it. I had used four sentences where one would do. Having read her note, I condensed the whole paragraph and sent it back the same evening.
Good writers, she says, use substitution rather than repetition. If you have written the old report once, the second time write the old one. If a colleague says she enjoyed the meeting and you enjoyed it too, say so did I rather than repeating the entire sentence. English allows both forms, but the shorter one always sounds more natural.
Some students find this advice ambiguous, and I did too at first. Yet the principle is simple. Say it once, clearly; if the reader can supply the missing words, leave them out.

tasks.text:
The implementation of the new water regulation began in March. Its evaluation, however, will not take place until next year, and that delay has already attracted criticism.
The report identifies three problems. The first is the allocation of funds. The distribution of money between the districts followed the old classification of regions, and no justification for that decision appears in the documents. The second problem is supervision. The administration of the programme was divided between two offices, and the coordination of their work was weak from the very start.
The third problem concerns transparency. Public access to the figures required a written request, and the verification of those figures by an independent body never took place. According to the authors, the absence of accountability made any interpretation of the results almost impossible.
The recommendations themselves are short. They call for the integration of the two offices, the introduction of a single reporting standard, and the adaptation of the timetable to the real speed of the work. Compliance with that standard would be checked twice a year. The transformation, the authors admit, will be slow.

tasks.text:
Researchers who study sleep tend to be cautious about their own conclusions. A recent paper postulates that short afternoon naps improve memory, yet the authors describe the finding as tentative rather than final. Their sample was relatively small, and the effect they measured was somewhat weaker than earlier work had suggested. The result may well be genuine, they write, but it does not yet warrant a firm claim.
Such caution is not weakness. When a team speculates in public without marking the claim as provisional, readers remember the headline and forget the doubt. A plausible idea then hardens into an accepted fact, and later studies that disagree with it are treated as strange exceptions. Broadly speaking, the language of science is designed to prevent exactly that. Expressions such as appear to, seemingly and roughly are not decoration; they carry information about how much confidence the evidence supports.
Students often find this style frustrating. They want a clear answer, and they read hedging as evasion. Yet a qualified statement that survives testing is far more useful than a confident one that collapses. Virtually every durable theory began as a cautiously worded proposal.

tasks.text:
Every large organisation eventually discovers that good intentions are not enough. A rule that lives only in conversation is forgotten within a month, so serious institutions write their expectations down. The result is a statute, a protocol or a simple set of clauses that anyone can consult.
Our university revised its admission procedure last autumn. The academic board recommended that the old entrance test be replaced, and it insisted that every applicant meet the same threshold. One member proposed that the interview be recorded, so that a rejected candidate could ask for a review. It was also agreed that the language requirement be published a full year in advance, since a prerequisite announced in August helps nobody.
Not every proposal survived. A request that the fee be waived for all applicants was refused; the board demanded instead that the existing exemption be applied only to students with proven financial need. Some members of staff complained that the new document was pure formality. Others answered that formality is precisely the point: a written norm can be questioned and improved, while an unwritten habit cannot.

tasks.text:
Nobody enjoys writing a contingency plan. The work is slow, the scenarios feel unlikely, and the finished document usually sits in a drawer for years. Yet the value of such a plan appears only at the moment when everything else has already failed.
Our factory learned this during the storm of March. Power was lost for eleven hours, and the whole site would have been shut for a week had the reserve generator not started automatically. Had we not spent two uncomfortable days arguing about that generator the previous autumn, it would never have been bought at all. Were the same storm to arrive tomorrow, the disruption would be measured in minutes rather than days.
The lesson is not that every hazard can be predicted. It cannot. The lesson is that resilience is built from small, boring decisions taken long before the crisis. A buffer of spare parts, a second supplier, a printed list of telephone numbers: none of them looks impressive on a balance sheet. Should the worst eventuality arrive, however, they are the only things standing between a difficult week and a permanent collapse.

tasks.text:
Most students believe that a weak essay is caused by weak ideas. In my experience the opposite is more common: the ideas are perfectly sound, but the reader cannot follow the path between them. Cohesion, not intelligence, is what usually fails.
Consider a typical example. A student states a thesis in the first paragraph, offers an illustration in the second, and then, in the third, introduces a counterargument without any warning at all. The reader stops, goes back, and reads the page again. Nothing in the text is false; the difficulty is that the relationship between the paragraphs has never been made visible.
A few words solve most of this. That said, a connector is not decoration. Admittedly signals a concession; consequently signals a result; by contrast signals opposition. If the word does not match the actual relationship, it confuses the reader rather than helping.
In essence, the writer should be able to draw the shape of the argument before writing a single paragraph. An outline of four lines is enough. Once that structure exists, the transitions almost write themselves, and the finished text reads as one continuous piece of reasoning.

tasks.text:
Every language contains expressions whose meaning cannot be worked out from the separate words. If an English speaker tells you that a colleague let the cat out of the bag, no animal has escaped; a secret has simply been revealed. Learners who translate such phrases word by word arrive at nonsense, and they usually blame their dictionary.
The difficulty is not only the idiom itself. Two words may share a denotation and still carry very different undertones. Thin and skinny describe the same body, yet one is neutral and the other is unkind. That difference is called connotation, and no dictionary entry can fully teach it.
Irony makes the problem harder still. When a British colleague looks at a ruined project and calls it a slight setback, the words are literally false and the meaning is perfectly clear to everyone in the room. Understatement of this kind is a form of humour, not of confusion.
There is only one reliable method. Read widely, listen to the way people actually speak, and record each expression together with the situation in which you heard it. Learn the whole phrase, never the separate parts.

tasks.text:
Two messages can carry exactly the same information and still produce completely different reactions. Send it over when you can is perfectly clear; so is I would be grateful if you could forward the document at your convenience. The difference is register, and choosing the wrong one damages a relationship faster than a spelling mistake ever will.
Most learners are taught the formal style first and then use it everywhere. That is its own kind of error. A message full of ceremony to a close colleague sounds cold, and readers often hear arrogance where the writer intended courtesy. Register is not a ladder with polite at the top; it is a match between the words and the relationship.
Three signals matter most. The greeting tells the reader how much distance you assume. The length of your sentences tells them how much ceremony you expect. The verbs tell them whether you are asking or instructing; could you possibly and send me are worlds apart.
The practical advice is simple. Before writing, decide who the reader is and what you want from them. Then match the tone, and read the message once more before pressing send.

Statistics courses teach students to calculate a correlation long before they teach them to distrust one. That order is unfortunate. Rarely does a strong correlation, on its own, tell us anything about causation, and almost every serious mistake in applied research begins at exactly that point.
Consider a familiar example. In one large sample, the number of drowning accidents rose with the sale of ice cream. Not only did the two figures move together, they moved together for years. No sensible person concluded that ice cream is dangerous. A third variable, summer heat, explained both of them.
Particularly striking is how often the same error survives in professional work. A company observes that its best employees attend many meetings and concludes that meetings produce excellence. Only after careful scrutiny does the opposite explanation appear: senior staff are invited to more meetings because they are already valued.
Never before had so much data been available to so many people, and that is precisely why the discipline matters. A number without a plausible mechanism behind it is not evidence. It is an invitation to look further.

items.q: What does the word 'variable' mean in this text?
options: a company that collects public data
a mistake made by a young researcher
a rule that every statistician follows

items.q: What can we conclude from the last paragraph?
options: A number counts as evidence only with a plausible mechanism behind it.
The amount of available data has fallen in recent years.
Discipline matters less now that data is easy to obtain.
Every published number should be accepted without question.

tasks.text: Thank you all for coming this morning. I will present three results from the March study. Never before had our sample been so large: four thousand households took part in it. Particularly striking is the correlation between income and travel time. Rarely does a single variable explain so much. Not only did the effect appear in the city, it also appeared in the rural districts. Only after careful scrutiny did we accept the figure, so please treat it as reliable.
